newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Landslide rescuers lose time as debris shifts.
newsitem.headline: Landslide rescuers lose time as debris shifts.

text.p: Shifting rubble on Tuesday cost rescuers precious hours in their race against the weather to find eight people entombed in a landslide at an Australian ski village.

A big slab of concrete, one of several balancing precariously atop the debris at Thredbo ski village, slipped 30 centimetres (one foot) before dawn, forcing rescuers to scurry from the steep hillside for fear of another collapse.
"It could have toppled," police spokesman Mark Hargreaves told Reuters at Thredbo, in the picturesque Snowy Mountains about 400 km (250 miles) south of Sydney.

Hundreds of rescuers have been working around the clock, burrowing beneath the mass of broken concrete, twisted metal and dirt since Wednesday night, when the mountainside gave way, destroying two ski lodges and entombing 19 people.
Miraculously, ski instructor Stuart Diver, who was in bed with his wife in one of the lodges, was unearthed alive from a concrete tomb deep within the rubble on Saturday night.
Diver, 27, suffered frostbite to his feet but remained on Tuesday in a remarkably good condition in a hospital in nearby Canberra.

A 10th body was recovered at Thredbo on Monday night, but progress since then has been hampered by the threat of further slippage. Approaching rain, forecast to arrive on Wednesday night, is also weighing on rescuers' minds.

Rescuers began preparing on Monday night to cover the disaster area with large plastic tarpaulins, to prevent rainfall from further destabilising the slope and flooding the honeycomb of tunnels dug into the rubble in search of more survivors.
But a concrete slab, which on Tuesday could be seen dangling almost vertically over the face of the slope, suddenly moved.
"He (a rescuer) heard something and then heard the slab move and it dropped vertically about 30 cm and that's when we pulled everybody out," leading firefighter Ray Kelly told reporters.

After six freezing nights, including the night of the disaster, rescuers were trying to hasten their search, quitting the painstakingly slow process of tunnelling by hand in favour of removing the heavy debris with earth movers and a crane.
"Looking for survivors is the most important aspect, but we have to move a large amount of debris...," said police site controller Don Keene.
Police have declined to identify the 10 bodies -- six male and four female -- so far recovered.
On Monday, police revised down the number of people initially trapped in the landslide from 20 to 19, when a woman assumed to have been trapped turned up alive and well.
The woman was thought to have been swept off her feet by the landslide, after her husband reported her missing in the initial confusion.
The small, tightly knit community of Thredbo on Tuesday began to tread the slow and painful path to recovery, releasing a song to mark the disaster that has hit this winter playground.
Titled "Winter Grows Colder", the song will be released on compact disc in about a week and sold to raise money for a fund set up this week to help the families of victims.
It has been performed by former resort worker Jodie Young who, like others who worked here in past winters, rushed to Thredbo to lend a hand to villagers struggling to cope.
